## Why it matters

The dot product takes two lists of numbers and returns one number that says how
much they agree. That question comes up all over engineering and data:

- **Work done by a force.** A tow rope pulls a cart with 200 N, angled 30° above
  the road, while the cart rolls 10 m. Only the part of the pull along the road
  does work: 200 × 10 × cos 30° ≈ 1,732 J.
- **Solar panels.** A panel tilted 40° away from the sun's rays collects
  cos 40° ≈ 77% of the power it would get facing the sun square on.
- **A shopping bill.** Quantities (3, 2, 1) times prices ($1.50, $4.00, $2.25)
  gives 3 × 1.50 + 2 × 4.00 + 1 × 2.25 = $14.75.
- **A neuron in a neural network.** Every input times its weight, added up. Each
  score in [matrix multiply](matrix-multiply.qmd) is one dot product.
- **Search and recommendations.** Songs, products and documents are stored as
  long lists of numbers. The ones whose lists point the same way as yours count
  as similar.
- **Lighting in 3D graphics.** A surface is brightest when it faces the light. The
  dot product of the two directions sets the brightness, and a negative value
  means the surface faces away and sits in shadow.

The bill and the neuron use it as a **weighted sum**. The force, the panel and
search use it to ask **how well two directions line up**. They are the same
calculation, and the theory below shows why.

## The theory

Take two lists of numbers of the same length. Multiply them position by position
and add the results. That sum is the dot product.

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \dots + a_n b_n
$$

For a = (3, 4) and b = (2, 1): a · b = 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10.

Now draw each list as an arrow from the origin: a goes 3 right and 4 up, b goes
2 right and 1 up. The same number is also

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert \cos\theta
$$

the length of a, times the length of b, times the cosine of the angle between
them. Here that is 5 × 2.24 × cos 26.6° = 10. Four rules follow:

- **The two lists must be the same length.** Every number needs a partner.
- **The sign gives the direction.** Positive when the arrows point the same
  general way, zero when they are at right angles, negative when they point
  generally opposite ways.
- **The size grows with length.** Double a and a · b doubles. Divide by both
  lengths and you get **cosine similarity**, cos θ, which runs from −1 to 1 and
  measures direction only.
- **Order doesn't matter.** a · b = b · a.

## The problem

A drone maintenance team pulls the vibration log after every flight. The log
splits vibration into two frequency bands: the **rotor band**, at the rate the
propellers spin, and the **high band**, well above it. Each is measured as RMS
acceleration in m/s². Known faults leave known patterns, or *signatures*
(the numbers here are illustrative):

| Signature      | Rotor band (m/s²) | High band (m/s²) |
|:---------------|------------------:|-----------------:|
| Prop imbalance | 6                 | 1                |
| Bearing wear   | 1                 | 5                |

: Two fault signatures {.striped}

Two flights come in from the same drone. One flew hard into a headwind and logged
(9, 3). The other was a gentle survey flight and logged (3, 1). The pattern is
the same, just three times weaker. Which fault does each log point to?

A first try is to dot each log with each signature and pick the bigger score.
The hard flight scores 57 for prop imbalance; the gentle flight scores only 19.
That makes the gentle flight look three times healthier, when both logs show the
same fault. The raw dot product mixes up *how strong* the vibration is with
*what shape* it has. Cosine similarity keeps only the shape.

Switch between the hard and the gentle flight. The dot product drops from 57 to

## The math, minimal

For two lists of length n, both of shape (n,):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \\[4pt]
\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert &= \sqrt{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \\[4pt]
\cos\theta &= \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert}
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Shapes:** (n,) · (n,) → a single number. Here n = 2 bands; Run the code
  uses 3; the word lists inside a language model use thousands.
- **Length:** a dotted with itself is Pythagoras: 3² + 4² = 25, so ‖(3, 4)‖ = 5.
- **Shadow:** a's shadow on b is a · b / ‖b‖. That is the picture's rule,
  a · b = ‖b‖ × shadow, rearranged.
- **Cost:** n multiplications and n − 1 additions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why the two formulas give the same number

Expand the length of the gap between the two tips, a − b, with the sum formula:
‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2 a · b. The law of cosines says the same side of the
triangle is ‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2 ‖a‖ ‖b‖ cos θ. Compare the two and
a · b = ‖a‖ ‖b‖ cos θ.
:::

## Worked example

The hard flight is a = (9, 3). Score it against both signatures.

**Dot products.** Prop imbalance: 9 × 6 + 3 × 1 = 57. Bearing wear:
9 × 1 + 3 × 5 = 24.

**Lengths.** ‖a‖ = √(81 + 9) = √90 ≈ 9.49. Prop imbalance: √(36 + 1) = √37 ≈ 6.08.
Bearing wear: √(1 + 25) = √26 ≈ 5.10.

**Cosines.** Prop imbalance: 57 / (9.49 × 6.08) ≈ 0.99, an angle of about 9.0°.
Bearing wear: 24 / (9.49 × 5.10) ≈ 0.50, about 60.3°.

The gentle flight, (3, 1), is the hard flight divided by 3. Its dot products
are divided by 3 as well, and so is its length, so the cosines don't change:

|                                  | Prop imbalance (6, 1) | Bearing wear (1, 5) |
|:---------------------------------|----------------------:|--------------------:|
| Dot product, hard flight (9, 3)  | 57                    | 24                  |
| Dot product, gentle flight (3, 1) | 19                   | 8                   |
| **Cosine similarity, either flight** | **0.99**          | **0.50**            |

: Raw scores depend on how hard the drone flew; cosine similarity doesn't {.striped}

Both logs point to prop imbalance. The team balances the propellers before the
next flight.

## Run the code

In NumPy, `@` between two lists is the dot product. Edit anything and press
**Run** (or Ctrl+Enter).

```{=html}
<py-cell packages="numpy"><script type="text/x-python">
import numpy as np

# Vibration in two bands (m/s^2 RMS): rotor band, high band. Illustrative.
prop    = np.array([6.0, 1.0])   # prop imbalance signature
bearing = np.array([1.0, 5.0])   # bearing wear signature
hard    = np.array([9.0, 3.0])   # hard flight
gentle  = hard / 3               # same pattern, a third as strong

def cosine(a, b):
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

for name, flight in [("hard", hard), ("gentle", gentle)]:
    print(f"{name:6}  dot:    prop {flight @ prop:5.1f}   bearing {flight @ bearing:5.1f}")
    print(f"{'':6}  cosine: prop {cosine(flight, prop):5.2f}   bearing {cosine(flight, bearing):5.2f}")
</script></py-cell>
```

Real logs have more than two bands, and the formula doesn't change. Below, a
third band is added for the motors, and four flights are checked against three
faults at once. Dividing every row by its length first turns each dot product
into a cosine, so one [matrix multiply](matrix-multiply.qmd) scores every flight
against every fault.

```{=html}
<py-cell packages="numpy"><script type="text/x-python">
import numpy as np

# Three bands (m/s^2 RMS): rotor, motor, high. Illustrative.
names = ["prop imbalance", "loose motor mount", "bearing wear"]
signatures = np.array([[6.0, 1.5, 1.0],
                       [1.5, 6.0, 1.0],
                       [1.0, 1.5, 5.0]])    # (3 faults, 3 bands)
logs = np.array([[8.0, 3.0, 2.0],
                 [2.0, 2.5, 6.5],
                 [1.2, 3.1, 0.8],
                 [4.0, 3.5, 3.0]])          # (4 flights, 3 bands)

def unit(rows):
    return rows / np.linalg.norm(rows, axis=1, keepdims=True)

cos = unit(logs) @ unit(signatures).T       # (4, 3) @ (3, 3) -> (4, 3)
print(cos.round(2))
for i, row in enumerate(cos):
    print(f"flight {i + 1}: closest to {names[row.argmax()]} ({row.max():.2f})")
</script></py-cell>
```

Flights 1 to 3 each match one fault at 0.99. Flight 4's best match is only
0.84, because its vibration is spread across all three bands. That is a log to
hand to a person rather than trust to the closest match.

## Practice questions

**1.** What is (2, −1) · (1, 2), and what does it tell you about the two arrows?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
2 × 1 + (−1) × 2 = 0. The arrows are at right angles.
:::

**2.** Can you take the dot product of (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No. The third number, 3, has no partner. The lists must be the same length.
:::

**3.** A new flight logs (2, 6). Which signature does it match, and how closely?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Bearing wear. Its cosine with (1, 5) is 32 / (6.32 × 5.10) ≈ 0.99. With prop
imbalance, (6, 1), it is only 18 / (6.32 × 6.08) ≈ 0.47.
:::

**4.** A sled is pulled with a force of (30, 40) N, 30 N forward and 40 N
upward, and slides (5, 0) m along flat snow. How much work does the pull do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Work is force · displacement: 30 × 5 + 40 × 0 = 150 J. The upward 40 N does no
work, because the sled never moves up.
:::

**5.** You double both a and b. What happens to a · b, and to the cosine
similarity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
a · b grows four times, because every product a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>i</sub> doubles
twice. The cosine doesn't change: the lengths in the bottom of the fraction also
grow four times, and the directions stay the same.
:::
